title: Speaking With Confidence
author: Tim Newman
description: A podcast focused on overcoming imposter syndrome and becoming a powerful communicator, covering public speaking, soft skills, storytelling, and building confidence through practical strategies and expert insights.

episodes.title: Boosting Youth Communication: Essential Soft Skills Every Teen Needs for Success
episodes.summary: Tim talks with Rob Heller of BOOST Youth Alliance about the communication skills missing from school, technology's effect on young people, and practical ways to help teens build real confidence.

episodes.title: The Four-Step Reset for Handling Difficult Conversations After They End
episodes.summary: Tim lays out a four-step framework for processing a hard conversation once it's over: calming your nervous system, telling reflection apart from rumination, writing down what was actually said, and deciding deliberately whether to follow up.

episodes.title: Turning Failure Into Fortune: The Power of Resilience, Focus, and Support Circles
episodes.summary: David Nassief shares a late-career layoff and his financial recovery, with a focus on emotional resilience and honest communication with family during a crisis.

episodes.title: How to Make Hard Conversations Safe, Productive, and Progress-Focused
episodes.summary: A three-step system for changing team conflict patterns, five positive communication habits, and how team cues help a group reset before disagreements escalate.

episodes.title: How Gen Z Changed My Mind About Communication and Connection
episodes.summary: Raquel Borras describes a cross-country RV trip making a Gen Z documentary, and what it taught her about stereotypes, pandemic-era communication gaps, and empathy across generations.

episodes.title: Five Dangerous Habits Destroying Your Communication Success
episodes.summary: Tim introduces the WRONG framework: five habits that sabotage conversations, including winning at all costs, reactive responses, dismissing other views, avoiding questions, and score-settling.

articles.question: How do you stop replaying a difficult conversation in your head?
articles.metaDescription: Tim Newman of Speaking With Confidence shares a four-step reset after a hard conversation: move 20 minutes, test for rumination, write it down.
articles.intro: You stop replaying a difficult conversation by giving your body time to clear the adrenaline, then giving your brain a job other than looping. On Speaking With Confidence, communication coach Tim Newman lays out a four-step reset: stop and move, run a reflection test, write down what was actually said, and make a deliberate follow-up decision. The whole thing takes less than an hour and is designed to keep one bad conversation from costing you a night's sleep.

sections.heading: Step 1: Move for 20 minutes before you think
sections.body:
The first step is physical, not mental. Tim explains that a tense conversation puts your body into fight-or-flight. It builds up energy to act, and if you sit at your desk afterward, that energy has nowhere to go.

So the first move is to stop and get moving. Walk, take the stairs, do anything that burns it off. He's specific about the time: about 20 minutes, because that's roughly how long it takes your body to clear most of the adrenaline it just dumped into your system.

Trying to analyze the conversation before that window closes is a mistake. You'll be thinking with a body that's still braced for a fight, and the conclusions you reach will reflect that.

quote.text: Your body built up energy to fight or take flight. If you don't move, that energy just sits there and buzzes in your chest until you burn it off some other way.
quote.speaker: Tim Newman

sections.heading: Step 2: The reflection test
sections.body:
Once you're calmer, you'll want to think it through. That's fine, but Tim draws a hard line between reflection and rumination. Reflection teaches you something. Rumination is the same clip on repeat.

His test is one question: am I learning something new, or am I just replaying the same moment again and again? If nothing new is showing up, you're ruminating, and more time won't help.

He also puts a timer on it. Five minutes, tops. If the lesson hasn't surfaced in five minutes, close the mental locker and walk away. You can come back later if there's genuinely something to learn, but the open-ended replay is what keeps people up at midnight.

quote.text: Set a timer for 5 minutes, tops. If the lesson hasn't shown up by then, you're ruminating with a stopwatch. Close the locker and walk away.
quote.speaker: Tim Newman

sections.heading: Step 3: Write the transcript, not the diary entry
sections.body:
The third step gets the conversation out of your head and onto paper, but Tim is precise about how. Write it like a transcript, both sides, using the actual words spoken as closely as you can remember them.

What you're not doing is writing a journal entry about how you felt. Feelings are real, but they're also what fuels the loop. When you write down the literal words, two things happen. You often discover the other person said less than you remember, and you get a record you can evaluate calmly instead of a feeling you keep re-experiencing.

This is also where the lesson from step two usually becomes obvious. Seeing your own words in writing makes it clear where you could have asked a question instead of reacting.

quote.text: Write out the conversation like a transcript, both sides. Not a journal entry about how you felt, the actual words that were spoken, as close as you can remember them.
quote.speaker: Tim Newman

sections.heading: Step 4: Decide, on purpose, whether to follow up
sections.body:
The final step is a decision, and Tim wants it made deliberately rather than by default. There are two valid outcomes.

If the relationship matters and the conversation felt incomplete, follow up within 24 to 48 hours. But the purpose is not to win the argument. He suggests a script that's almost boring on purpose: "I've been thinking about our conversation and want to make sure I understood you correctly." Your goal is to learn something, not reopen the fight.

If follow-up isn't warranted, then decide the conversation is over. The lesson is captured in your notes. Your energy belongs somewhere else now. Tim frames that decision as the difference between sleeping well and staring at the ceiling, and he's clear that not deciding is what leaves the door open for the replay to start again.

quote.text: You don't follow up to win. If the relationship matters and the conversation felt incomplete, follow up within 24 to 48 hours.
quote.speaker: Tim Newman

keyTakeaways: Move your body for about 20 minutes first; that's how long it takes to clear the adrenaline.
Ask whether you're learning something new. If not, you're ruminating, and five minutes is the limit.
Write the conversation as a transcript of what was said, not a journal entry about how you felt.
If you follow up, do it within 24 to 48 hours and go in to understand, not to win.
If you don't follow up, consciously declare the conversation over so your brain can let it go.

faq.q: Why can't I stop thinking about an argument?
faq.a: Tim's explanation is that your body is still carrying the adrenaline from the conversation and your mind is replaying instead of reflecting. Moving for 20 minutes and then running the five-minute reflection test breaks both halves of that loop.

faq.q: Should I text someone after a difficult conversation?
faq.a: Only if the relationship matters and the conversation felt unfinished, and then within 24 to 48 hours. Keep it to something like "I want to make sure I understood you correctly" rather than restating your case.

faq.q: What's the difference between reflecting and ruminating?
faq.a: Reflection produces something new, a lesson or a different angle. Rumination replays the same moment without adding anything. If you can't name what you've learned, you're ruminating.
